analysis.one_liner: Requires food processors and importers to register, pass quarterly inspections, and recall unsafe food.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after two referrals it sat in a House subcommittee from May 1999 until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up a national food safety program for foods the FDA oversees. Every food processing plant and importer would have to register, put pathogen controls in place, and pass unannounced inspections at least four times a year. The government would get power to order contaminated food recalled, fine violators up to $100,000 per act, protect whistleblowers, and tighten checks on imported food. It was introduced by Rep. Frank Pallone and referred to the House Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee and never acted on it again.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats FDA-regulated food. The bill aimed to reduce foodborne illness by forcing processing plants and importers to adopt preventive controls, subject them to quarterly unannounced inspections, and give the Health and Human Services Department mandatory recall authority over contaminated products. It would also have protected employees who report unsafe practices and let citizens sue violators.

how_it_helps.text: Required every food processing facility and importer to register with the Health and Human Services Department, giving regulators a full list of who handles the food supply.
Mandated unannounced inspections at least quarterly of processing and importing facilities, with reduced frequency only for plants the Secretary certified as negligible-risk.

Directed the Secretary to issue regulations setting sanitation standards, contaminant tolerances, process controls, recordkeeping, and sampling so plants prevent contamination rather than respond to it after people get sick.
Gave the Secretary authority to order a mandatory recall of food found to present a public health threat, after a voluntary recall opportunity and a hearing within two days.
Allowed civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, with each continuing day a separate offense, and prohibited retaliation against whistleblowers.

Required a comprehensive import safety system, including routine inspection of foreign processing facilities and ports of entry, and certification of exporting nations whose safety programs match U.S. protection levels.

Let any person sue a violator in federal court to enforce food safety rules, with possible attorney's fees, and required contaminant tolerances to account for sensitive groups such as children, the elderly, pregnant women, and the immune-compromised.
Set up national surveillance, public education, and research programs to track and explain foodborne illness sources.

analysis.who_pays: Food processing companies and food importers, who would bear the cost of registration, pathogen controls, recordkeeping, sampling, more frequent inspections, and penalties for violations. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through prices. Taxpayers would fund the inspection force, surveillance, and research through appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for registration, process controls, recordkeeping, and up to quarterly inspections would fall on food processors and importers of all sizes, and small plants could face proportionally heavier burdens than large ones; some of these costs would likely show up in grocery prices.

The bill's citizen-suit provision lets any person sue a violator for damages and attorney's fees, and its penalty structure allows $100,000 per act per day, which critics of similar regimes warn can invite litigation and inflate regulatory costs beyond the health benefit.

The bill authorized 'such sums as may be necessary' rather than a fixed budget, leaving the size of the new inspection and surveillance apparatus to later appropriations and creating an unfunded mandate risk if Congress did not appropriate the money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, broad harm: foodborne illness from pathogens and contaminants in FDA-regulated food, which the existing law of the time addressed mainly through sparse inspections and largely voluntary recalls. The main costs were compliance and inspection spending, partly passed to consumers as slightly higher food prices, plus a citizen-suit and penalty regime that could generate litigation. On balance it was a consumer-protection bill whose costs fell on a specific industry and whose benefits were spread across everyone who eats; its design details, such as open-ended appropriations, would have needed attention in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health and Environment subcommittee on May 17, 1999, and neither the subcommittee nor the full committee ever held a vote on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on April 28, 1999, joined by 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce.
On May 17, 1999, the committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a subcommittee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill's 17 cosponsors included 16 Democrats and 1 Independent, with no Republican support, on a committee controlled at the time by the opposing party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food processing companies and importers came out ahead: they avoided mandatory registration, quarterly unannounced inspections, government-ordered recalls, and penalties of up to $100,000 per violation that the bill would have imposed. Consumers gained nothing, since the safety program never took effect.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents, with no Republican support, and the bill died in a committee then controlled by Republicans without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required plants to register, adopt pathogen controls, keep detailed records, and pass unannounced inspections up to four times a year, with civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation per day. Its defeat spared processors those compliance costs, while consumers got no new safety guarantees.

Importers faced registration, port-of-entry inspection, and detention of suspect shipments, and exporting nations would have needed U.S.-certified safety systems to keep selling into the country. Blocking the bill preserved the lighter-touch import regime then in place.

The bill would have obligated anyone in the distribution chain to notify regulators of suspected unsafe food and to participate in recalls. The burden is modest but real; so is the benefit of faster removal of contaminated products from shelves.
